miniProject.title: Tensor reverse-mode engine with differential checks
miniProject.brief: Build a small tensor autodiff engine on NumPy in your own repository: broadcast-aware operations, reverse accumulation over branched graphs, a stable cross-entropy and one tensor MLP. Prove its gradients against finite differences and PyTorch, not against a training curve.
steps: Implement a Tensor class on NumPy with add, mul, matmul, sum over axes, exp, log, tanh and ReLU, each with a backward rule, and a backward() that visits a topological order and accumulates into .grad.
Make every binary op broadcast-aware: sum each incoming gradient over the broadcast axes back to the operand shape. Test (3, 1) with (1, 4), (4,) with (3, 4), and a scalar, against PyTorch.

Add log-softmax and mean cross-entropy as one fused op whose gradient is softmax minus one-hot over the batch size. Test float32 logits of magnitude 1000 for finite loss and gradients, against torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy.

Build a branched graph where one tensor reaches the loss through at least three paths, one of them broadcast, for example L = sum(x * w + x.sum(0) * b + tanh(x)). Check every leaf gradient against central differences and against PyTorch, both in float64, with a step and tolerance you justify.
Train a two-layer tensor MLP with your engine on a small synthetic classification set, and show its first-step gradients match a PyTorch copy with the same weights.

Layout tests: feed transposed and noncontiguous arrays into your engine and match gradients from contiguous copies. For PyTorch views, assert shared storage through untyped_storage().data_ptr(), and compute the element offset from strides and storage_offset for a slice, a transpose and an expand.

Reproduce one saved-value or mutation defect, such as an input edited in place between forward and backward. Show the wrong or refused gradient, fix it with a copy on save or a version counter, and keep a regression test.
deliverables: The engine package: ops with broadcast-aware backward, topological backward, fused cross-entropy and the MLP.
The test suite: float64 finite-difference and PyTorch checks, broadcast cases, extreme-logit cases, layout and storage tests, and the defect regression test.
A one-page note listing the values each op saves for backward, why, and the tolerance chosen for each check.

checks.name: TensorTonic autograd-from-scratch problems named in the units
checks.note: Free plan. Solve the dense layer, tanh, topological sort, shared-path accumulation and gradient-check problems before you wire the same rules into your engine.

rubric.pass: Every op matches PyTorch in float64 within a stated tolerance on random inputs.
rubric.strong: The branched broadcast graph matches both finite differences and PyTorch, and the note justifies the step size and tolerance.

rubric.pass: Gradients reduce to each operand shape in the tested broadcast cases.
rubric.strong: A property test draws random broadcast-compatible shape pairs and compares against PyTorch.

rubric.pass: Cross-entropy is finite for float32 logits of magnitude 1000.
rubric.strong: A test shows the naive form failing on the same input, and the note explains why the max shift leaves the gradient unchanged.

rubric.pass: One defect is reproduced, fixed and guarded by a test.
rubric.strong: The note lists every saved value per op, and the engine either refuses or survives an in-place edit of a saved input, with a test for each case.

rubric.pass: Transposed and noncontiguous inputs give the same gradients as contiguous copies.
rubric.strong: Storage and offset assertions cover a slice, a transpose and an expand, checked against PyTorch strides.
